newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - Australia wool exports seen up in 96/7-ABARE.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Australia wool exports seen up in 96/7-ABARE.

text.p: Australia's official commodities forecaster, the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE), has raised its forecast for Australian wool exports in 1996/97 but held its forecast of production steady.
Exports of Australian wool are forecast to rise by about 13 percent in 1996/97 (June 30) to 889,000 tonnes, ABARE said.
This is up on ABARE's previous forecast of 813,000 tonnes.
The value of exports is forecast at A$3.84 billion, up on the previous forecast of A$3,55 billion.
In 1995/96, Australia exported 788,000 tonnes of wool on a greasy equivalent basis, worth A$3.62 billlion.

Exports of Australian wool to all major markets, Japan and South Korea particularly, were expected to increase as processors re-build stocks and increase processing activity, ABARE said in its latest forecast.
ABARE noted that the Australian Wool Production Forecasting Committee had forecast that shorn wool production would fall by nearly 5,000 tonnes to 641,200 tonnes in 1996/97.
This is steady with ABARE's June forecast of Australian wool production for the year.
Higher production in New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania was expected to be more than offset by falls in other states, ABARE said.

Wool production is forecast to fall by nearly five percent in South Australia and Western Australia as a result of lower average fleece weights and reduced numbers of sheep shorn. A further fall in Queensland production was expected following poor seasonal conditions in northerrn wool producing areas.
Any improvement in demand and the potential for price increases was expected to result in increased quantities of wool being released from private stocks, ABARE said.
ABARE is forecasting flat wool prices with the eastern market indicatior forecast to be similar to the 1995/96 average at 620 cents/kg in 1996/97.

"Although improving economic conditions in the major wool buying countries will mean strengthening demand for raw wool, the expected increase of wool available for sale in Australia in 1996/97 is likely to largely offset the potential for price rises," the forecaster said.
The expected increase in wool supply, despite a forecast fall in production, was a result of a large increase in stocks of unsold wool in brokers' stores and on farms since last season, ABARE said.
Prices for fine wool types were expected to benefit from improved demand, principally from Japan and Western Europe, and tighter supply in 1996/97, the report said.
